prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose oeuvre that builds whole inner cosmologies from memory, the body and dream, with roots in poetry.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading my colleagues' openings. The case for Cărtărescu rests on the common criteria, not on the fact that the openings converge. His voice is distinctive. Public knowledge of Blinding (the Orbitor sequence) and Solenoid supports a sustained formal project: long architectural structures, recurring image systems, and memory, the body and dream treated as a metaphysical subject. The poetry and essays suggest one imaginative enterprise across genres, with a lineage that runs through Romantic and modernist visionary traditions. The oeuvre appears consolidated, since Solenoid is widely seen as a late culmination, so the question is not premature judgment. A single-writer citation is clear: the large-scale visionary novel, not one title and not national symbolism. I would still treat this as a literary argument that has to be tested against the strongest alternatives, not as a settled outcome.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the case rests on dense, rhythmic Romanian prose that I can judge only through translation, and that the longest, most digressive books may divide readers between depth and excess. Coverage of the early poetry and shorter work in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so the claim of one coherent oeuvre across genres is partly inferred. Sustained quality across the whole body of work, not only the peak novels, needs closer examination.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first but warns that the citation must place him in Romanian and European literature without reducing him to a generic 'postmodern' label. She also notes that the longest works are demanding and that their durability as a whole is a judgment call.
responses.response: I agree with both points. A citation should name the visionary, metaphysical architecture of the prose and its roots in poetry, and should avoid a period label that says little. I would qualify her second point: durability across the longest works cannot be settled from public reputation alone. I accept that this is a real uncertainty and have kept it as my main reservation. It does not change my preference, but it does argue for a citation that rests on the oeuvre's imaginative project and not on any single volume.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Carson second and sees formal reinvention at the meeting of poetry, classical translation and essay. She flags that the genre-crossing makes the scope of the achievement harder to define.
responses.response: I share her concern about scope, which is why I place Carson fourth and not higher. Autobiography of Red and Nox show real formal invention and intellectual depth. But a lifetime citation needs a defined body of literary work, and the line between original work, scholarship and translation is hard to draw here. Cărtărescu's scope is easier to state. I do not think this makes Carson lesser as a writer, only harder to cite. If the committee can define the scope around the original poetic work, I would take the case more seriously than my ranking suggests.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Michon third for compressed, syntactically sculpted prose of very high language-level achievement, and acknowledges that the small body of work raises a question about breadth. He ranks Can Xue last among his eight.
responses.response: I agree that Michon's sentence-level achievement is very high, and I would not call the small oeuvre a flaw. But the criterion is significance across a body of work, and that is where I hesitate, in addition to the loss in translating a style that depends on the French sentence. I rank him fifth. On Can Xue I differ from his placement. Her method is consistent over decades, and he reads that as a question about development. I read it as sustained distinctiveness, though I accept that the question of variation within it is legitimate and that my ranking depends on translations of only part of a large corpus.

responses.point: Sward ranks Tawada second, arguing that bilingual writing in Japanese and German makes linguistic estrangement a formal principle across several genres, and that the corpus must be assessed in both languages.
responses.response: Her point about assessing both languages is the right standard, and it is also the reason I did not rank Tawada in my opening eight. The premise of linguistic estrangement as method is serious, and The Emissary and Memoirs of a Polar Bear point to real formal intelligence. But I cannot judge from public knowledge how the German and Japanese bodies of work compare in quality, or how well wordplay survives translation. I would want to hear more on how she weighs the earlier and later work before moving Tawada into my alternatives.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's density, musicality and rhythm survives translation, and whether the longest novels sustain quality throughout.
Translation coverage of his poetry, essays and early work, which weakens the claim of a single coherent oeuvre across genres.
Whether Can Xue's consistent method reads as rigor or repetition, given partial translation of a very large corpus.
For Adonis, how far the achievement in Arabic prosody and form can be judged through translation, and how to keep the literary case separate from his public political positions.
How to define the scope of a citation for Carson, given the boundaries between original work, scholarship and translation.
I have not independently verified any bibliography and rely on general public knowledge of the works named.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own scholarly and poetic interests (modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature, Celan) are context and not evidence of any preference. The documented connections listed (Engdahl, Birnbaum, the Kris circle) do not involve any shortlisted writer.
